title: Runtime Noise Sensitivity & Kernel Selection Study
summary: Customer and Redwood SE ran through reproducible tail-latency spikes seen on OmniHealth's on-prem cluster. Focus: isolating noise sources (NVLink jitter, cudagraph capture/replay, kernel choice thresholds) and designing a bisect experiment that avoids masking by warmup or caching. Agreed next steps: run deterministic-capture sweep, collect nvprof + nsight warp traces, and test quantized vs fp16 kernel paths with/without KV prefetch; Redwood to provide config snippets and a telemetry checklist.

Schedule follow-up triage to review traces and p95/p99 anomalies week of 2026-11-30

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62m
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recording/ff-20261118-rns-4b7q

Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Jesse (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood Solutions), Maria (OmniHealth VP Eng), Priya (ML Eng), Ethan (SRE), Noah (Infra)

--- Optional auto-summary (auto) ---
Summary (auto-generated): Customer sees intermittent p99 spikes on on-prem cluster when running quantized int8 models through TRT-LLM path. Suspected sources: NVLink jitter, cudagraph replay nondeterminism, KV cache warmup corner cases.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: hey everybody thanks for taking the time, quick intros. we got Jesse on the call to go deep on the repro you shared and figure out where the tail is coming from.
[00:14] Maria: thanks, yes the p50 is fine but once we run sustained traffic we see these spikes that blow our sla out, uh, primarily on the dedicated on-prem cluster, nvlink interconnect between the four blades.
[00:30] Jesse: cool, can you confirm you're hitting the tensorrt-llm path or vllm? earlier note said TRT-LLM compiled int8.
[00:36] Priya: yeah, we've been trying TRT-LLM int8. we also tested vllm fp16 briefly — vllm is more stable but cost is higher.
[00:47] Lina: and are you using KV cache persistent across requests or recreating per-call? that often changes pressure.
[00:53] Priya: we're persisting the KV in memory but we prefetch the prefix for long-horizon prompts; there might be an eviction or a prefetch race.
[01:05] Ethan: i pulled dmesg and there are occasional NVLink timeouts logged but nothing catastrophic, more like transient stalls.
[01:13] Noah: also driver is 525.x, but we've seen variant behavior on 525 vs 535 on other clusters.
[01:20] Jesse: okay this matches classic noise sensitivity: a small jitter in nvlink or cudagraph background replay can flip which kernel the runtime picks; once you hit a different kernel path it may allocate different workspace sizes and that can cascade into a tail spike.
[01:36] Maria: can you explain the kernel flip part, because to us ``kernel selection" sounds low level but the app-level is just latency jump.
[01:45] Jesse: yeah sure — at runtime we have heuristics that choose an execution kernel variant based on seq len distribution and available workspace. if a prefetch stalls or the cudagraph capture fails partially, the runtime falls back to a more general kernel which is slower and has worse concurrency. small timing noise can therefore create a bimodal latency distribution.
[02:06] Samir: also worth noting cache fragmentation from quantization paths — int8 kernels might use different memory banks, nha, the allocator may put KV pages on a different bank which affects NVLink hops.
[02:18] Priya: we did see that when we forced int8 we sometimes got a few unusually high alloc latencies in profiler.
[02:26] Jesse: right, so plan is to bisect: isolate (A) cudagraph capture/replay vs no-cudagraph, (B) kv prefetch behavior (prefetch up front / delayed / disabled), (C) kernel locking (force kernel variant) and (D) driver versions.
[02:40] Lina: for kernel locking we can supply a config to force the TRT-LLM optimized kernel path; that removes heuristic flips and often stabilizes tail.
[02:49] Ethan: curious, will forcing a kernel reduce throughput? we need p95 but not sacrifice sustained throughput.
[02:56] Jesse: sometimes forcing a kernel reduces peak throughput because you lose a faster specialized kernel for some sequences, but in practice for long-horizon prompts the stability tradeoff is worth it. we should measure tokens/sec too.
[03:10] Maria: ok, what telemetry should we capture? we've been sending basic logs.
[03:16] Jesse: minimum: nvprof/nsight warp traces with NVTX ranges around request lifecycle, cudagraph capture/replay timestamps, kernel selection markers (we'll add a flag to log kernel id), GPU memory allocator traces, and system-level (dmesg, nvidia-smi topo, network stats). Preferably capture for the full 30 minute sustained run.
[03:35] Priya: will you provide a sample harness? we can integrate into our CI.
[03:39] Samir: yes we'll push a small repro harness that uses your promptset and toggles prefetch and cudagraph flags. Jesse will attach deterministic capture example.
[03:47] [04:00] -- brief cross-talk about dates and Slack channel --
[04:20] Jesse: one gotcha: cudagraph capture is nondeterministic if you have dynamic shapes or racey prefetch; deterministic capture requires a fixed warmup sequence and pinned streams. we'll include an example that pins two CUDA streams and performs a fixed warmup phase of 64 tokens before capture.
[04:37] Noah: does that warmup hide the rare spike though? we've been skeptical that warmup just masks the root cause.
[04:44] Jesse: valid — which is why we do two runs: a cold-capture run (no warmup) to surface capture-time nondeterminism, and a production-like warmed prefix run to see steady-state. differences between those runs point to capture-time issues vs steady-state kernel divergence.
[05:00] Lina: also, instrument the allocator to show which memory bank pages used; it will reveal if int8 path moves working set across NVLink boundaries.
[05:09] Priya: ok we'll add the nvlink counters Ethan mentioned.
[05:14] Maria: relationship to vllm? our ops folks pushed vllm because it was more stable but management wants to understand cost/benefit.
[05:22] Jesse: vllm and TRT-LLM differ: vllm uses a memory-friendly dynamic runtime with different batching semantics; TRT-LLM compiles optimized kernels which are higher throughput but more brittle to graph capture and allocator layout. for your workload with long sequences vllm sometimes wins on tail, TRT-LLM wins on median throughput; so it's a tradeoff.
[05:46] Samir: we should also try a hybrid: route short/cold requests to vllm and long/steady to TRT-LLM, Redwood Smart Routing can do that; but that adds routing complexity.
[05:58] Ethan: what about quantization differences? int8 can change numerical stability, but here it's more about memory bank usage and cuda kernel choices.
[06:07] Jesse: yes int8 can alter which kernel is selected (specialized int8 kernels). also watch out for mixed-precision ephemeral tensors causing spikes when fallback to fp16 occurs.
[06:20] Priya: any known driver versions to avoid? we saw differences 525 vs 535 as Noah mentioned.
[06:26] Jesse: latest 535.x addressed some NVLink retry bugs; but some cudagraph replay fixes landed earlier. we'll include a driver matrix to test. don't upgrade production until we test.
[06:36] Maria: can you walk us through the exact bisect plan now?
[06:41] Jesse: sure. Step 1: reproducible baseline run with your promptset with current config (we'll attach a dockerized harness). Step 2: disable cudagraph capture entirely and re-run — compare p95/p99 and kernel id logs. Step 3: enable cudagraph but force deterministic capture (pinned streams + fixed warmup) — if that changes behavior, capture-time nondeterminism is the culprit. Step 4: toggle KV prefetch modes: prefetch-on, prefetch-delayed (after token 128), prefetch-off. Step 5: force kernel locking (force int8 kernel if available) and repeat. Step 6: vary driver (525 vs 535) and nvlink stress test. For each run collect NVTX, nsight, kernel ids, allocator traces and attach.
[07:45] Maria: sounds actionable. how long will these take?
[07:50] Jesse: each run about 30 minutes; if you parallelize runs across nodes you can finish in a day or two. but capturing nsight can be heavy, so probably spread out.
[08:00] Samir: we'll provide a checklist of flags and a sample config. Lina will also add Redwood Console dashboard view that surfaces kernel id and p99 correlation so you can watch in realtime.
[08:12] Priya: about telemetry retention — we don't want to store full nsight traces forever. do you have guidance?
[08:18] Lina: keep full traces for triage windows, upload compressed when needed; Redwood Console can ingest summary stats and NVTX markers without storing raw traces. we'll include sample compression commands.
[08:30] Ethan: are there known heuristics for when to prefer vllm vs trt-llm automatically?
[08:36] Jesse: yes, rule-of-thumb: if your median seq len < 128 and you need high throughput, trt-llm usually wins. for median > 256 or highly variable seq length, vllm often has better tail. But these are heuristics — that's why we measure.
[08:54] Maria: ok, and security/compliance side — we're on VPC with private deployment. any additional constraints?
[09:00] Samir: none for this triage; keep telemetry within your private bucket. Redwood SEs will supply scripts you can run in-cluster.
[09:08] Priya: quick question: you mentioned pinned streams earlier — is that safe with multi-tenant Dedicated?
[09:15] Jesse: pinned streams are per-process; on multi-tenant you may not want to alter affinity. for Dedicated you can safely pin. we'll add an alternative capture that uses stream tagging without changing affinity.
[09:26] Maria: cool. anything else?
[09:29] Noah: we saw occasional leakage in allocator stats; memory pressure pattern looked like fragmentation rather than leak.
[09:35] Jesse: that aligns with kernel switching causing different temp allocations. in the traces look for increasing fragmentation after kernel flip events.
[09:45] Priya: practical ask — can Redwood share a small sample of kernel id mapping so we know which kernel id corresponds to which compiled variant?
[09:53] Samir: yes we'll share a mapping file; Jesse will also add a runtime flag to log human-friendly kernel names.
[10:02] Maria: any estimated risk that forcing kernel will be harmful to model quality?
[10:07] Jesse: forcing kernel only affects execution path, not model weights, so no quality change. quantization mode choice could affect outputs but that's separate.
[10:15] Samir: okay we're at about 40 minutes in front of the detailed plan, want to make sure next steps and owners are captured.
[10:22] Maria: yep please share the harness and the checklist.
[10:25] Jesse: i'll upload the deterministic capture example to the shared drive, link will be in the follow-up email. it includes the pinned-stream example, NVTX markup, and kernel-lock flag.
[10:35] Samir: we'll also create a temporary Redwood Console dashboard that watches kernel id vs p95 and give you read access.
[10:40] Maria: perfect. thanks everyone.
